series-convergence-s1.title: Partial sums of a series

plot.label: Partial sums S sub n of a series for n = 1 to 10, rising toward the dashed line at height 3

series-convergence-s1.text: The graph shows the partial sums $S_n = \frac{3n}{n + 2}$ of a series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n$, for $n = 1$ to $10$. The dashed line is at height 3.

series-convergence-s2.title: A series whose partial sums jump

items.q: What is the sum of the series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n$?

mistakes.why: That is $S_1 = a_1$, the first partial sum. The sum is where the partial sums head as $n$ grows.
That is the limit of the terms $a_n$. The sum of the series is the limit of the partial sums $S_n$.

why.correct: The sum of a series is the limit of its partial sums: $\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{3n}{n + 2} = 3$.

items.q: Find $a_3$, the third term of the series.

mistakes.why: That is $S_3$, the sum of the first three terms. The third term alone is $S_3 - S_2$.

why.correct: $a_3 = S_3 - S_2 = \frac{9}{5} - \frac{3}{2} = \frac{3}{10}$: the third partial sum minus the second.

items.q: Write the general term $a_n$ of the series in terms of $n$.

mistakes.why: That is $S_n$, the sum of the first $n$ terms. The $n$th term is $S_n - S_{n-1}$.
Subtract the whole previous partial sum: $a_n = \frac{3n}{n + 2} - \frac{3(n - 1)}{n + 1}$, over a common denominator.

items.q: Which statement about this series is correct?
options: The terms converge to 3, so the series converges
The series diverges, since $S_n$ keeps growing as $n$ grows
The series converges to 3, and its terms approach 0
The series converges to 3, and its terms approach 3

why.correct: A series converges when its partial sums have a limit; here $S_n \to 3$, so the series converges, to 3. Say it about the series: \"the series converges\", not \"the terms converge to 3\".
options: The terms approach 0, not 3. It is the partial sums that approach 3.
Partial sums can rise forever and still approach a limit; here they level off at 3.
Right: the partial sums approach 3, and $a_n = \frac{6}{(n + 1)(n + 2)} \to 0$.
If every term were near 3, the partial sums would grow by about 3 each step and never level off.

mistakes.why: That is the sum from $n = 1$. Starting at $n = 5$ leaves out $a_1 + a_2 + a_3 + a_4 = S_4 = 2$.
That subtracts $S_5 = \frac{15}{7}$, which includes $a_5$. Subtract only the terms before $n = 5$: $S_4$.

why.correct: Leave out the first four terms: $\sum_{n=5}^{\infty} a_n = S - S_4 = 3 - \frac{12}{6} = 1$.

items.q: Find $S_{100}$, the sum of the first 100 terms.

mistakes.why: Odd partial sums are 1; with an even number of terms, every 1 is canceled by a $-1$.
The terms are not all 1: they alternate between 1 and $-1$.

why.correct: The terms pair off as $(1 - 1) + (1 - 1) + \cdots$; 100 terms make 50 pairs, each 0, so $S_{100} = 0$. Every even partial sum is 0.

options: Yes, to 0, since the even partial sums are 0
Yes, to 1, since the first term is 1
Yes, since each term is 1 or $-1$ and so stays bounded
No: the partial sums jump between 1 and 0

why.correct: $S_n$ is 1 for odd $n$ and 0 for even $n$. The sequence of partial sums has no limit, so the series diverges.
options: The odd partial sums are 1; the whole sequence of partial sums has no limit.
The sum of a series is the limit of all its partial sums, not its first term.
Bounded partial sums are not enough; they must approach a single number.
Right: a series converges when its partial sums approach one number, and these do not.

items.q: A student writes $(1 - 1) + (1 - 1) + \cdots = 0$, and then $1 + (-1 + 1) + (-1 + 1) + \cdots = 1$. What is the flaw?
options: The first grouping is right, so the sum is 0
The second grouping is right, so the sum is 1
Regrouping the terms changes the partial sums; the series has no sum
Both are right, so the sum is the average, $\frac{1}{2}$

why.correct: The sum of a series is $\lim_{n \to \infty} S_n$. Grouping keeps only some partial sums (every other one), and here those choices disagree because $\lim S_n$ does not exist: the series diverges.
options: Grouping picks out the even partial sums only; the odd ones are 1.
Grouping this way picks out the odd partial sums only; the even ones are 0.
Right: each grouping looks at a different selection of partial sums, and the full sequence of partial sums has no limit.
A sum is a limit of partial sums, not an average of two groupings.

items.q: A student says the sum of this series is $\frac{1}{2}$, the average of the values of $S_n$. Is that correct?
options: Yes: the partial sums center on $\frac{1}{2}$
No: the series diverges, so it has no sum
No: the sum is 0, from the even partial sums
No: the sum is 1, the first partial sum

why.correct: A series has a sum only when its partial sums approach a number. These jump between 1 and 0 forever, so the series diverges and has no sum.
options: Centering is not converging; the partial sums never get close to $\frac{1}{2}$.
Right: with no limit of the partial sums, there is no sum to report.
Half the partial sums are 1; choosing the even ones is arbitrary.
The first partial sum is not the sum of the whole series.

mistakes.why: Two positive pieces survive the canceling, $1$ and $\frac{1}{2}$, because each term cancels with the one two places later.
That is $S_1 = 1 - \frac{1}{3}$. The sum is the limit of $S_n$ as $n \to \infty$.

items.q: The partial sums of a series are $S_n = \frac{n^2}{n^2 + 1}$. Find the fourth term, $a_4$.

mistakes.why: That is $S_4$, the sum of the first four terms. Subtract $S_3$ to get the fourth term alone.
That is the sum of the series, $\lim S_n$, not a single term.

items.q: The partial sums of $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \ln\left(\frac{n + 1}{n}\right)$ are $S_n = \ln(n + 1)$. What does this show?
options: The series converges, since its terms approach 0
The series converges to $\ln 2$, its first term
The series diverges, though its terms approach 0
The series converges to 0

why.correct: $S_n = \ln 2 - \ln 1 + \ln 3 - \ln 2 + \cdots = \ln(n + 1) \to \infty$, so the series diverges, even though each term $\ln\left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right)$ approaches 0.
options: Terms approaching 0 do not make a series converge: these partial sums grow forever.
$\ln 2$ is $a_1 = S_1$. The sum would be $\lim S_n$, which does not exist.
Right: $\ln(n + 1)$ grows without bound, while $\ln\left(1 + \frac{1}{n}\right) \to 0$.
The terms approach 0; the partial sums grow without bound.

items.q: For a series $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n$, what is the partial sum $S_n$?
options: The $n$th term, $a_n$
The sum of the first $n$ terms, $a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_n$
The sum of the terms after the $n$th one
The limit of $a_n$ as $n \to \infty$

why.correct: $S_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k$. The series converges to $S$ exactly when $\lim_{n \to \infty} S_n = S$.
options: $a_n$ is one term; $S_n$ adds the first $n$ of them.
Right: the series converges when these partial sums have a limit.
That is what is left over, $S - S_n$, when the series converges.
That limit describes the terms, not the sum of the first $n$.

items.q: The partial sums of a series are $S_n = 5 - \frac{2}{n}$. Find the first term, $a_1$.

mistakes.why: That is the sum of the series, $\lim_{n \to \infty} S_n$. The first term is $S_1$.
2 is the amount subtracted at $n = 1$, not the term. The first term is the first partial sum: $a_1 = S_1 = 5 - \frac{2}{1} = 3$.

why.correct: $a_1 = S_1 = 5 - 2 = 3$. (The sum of the series is $\lim S_n = 5$.)

mistakes.why: Multiplying every term by 3 multiplies every partial sum, and so the sum, by 3.
A constant factor multiplies the sum; it is not added to it.

why.correct: Each partial sum is multiplied by 3, so the limit is $3 \cdot 4 = 12$.

items.q: $\sum a_n$ converges and $\sum b_n$ diverges. What can be said about $\sum (a_n + b_n)$?
options: It converges
It may converge or diverge
It diverges
It converges to $\sum a_n$

why.correct: Suppose $\sum (a_n + b_n)$ converged. Then $\sum b_n = \sum (a_n + b_n) - \sum a_n$ would be a difference of convergent series, which converges, a contradiction. So $\sum (a_n + b_n)$ diverges.
options: Adding a convergent series cannot cancel the divergence of $\sum b_n$.
This case is settled: the difference of two convergent series converges, so the sum here cannot.
Right: if it converged, $\sum b_n = \sum (a_n + b_n) - \sum a_n$ would converge too.
The terms $b_n$ do not drop out; they keep the partial sums from settling.

items.q: $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n$ converges to 10, and $a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_{99} = 7$. What is true of $\sum_{n=100}^{\infty} a_n$?
options: It converges, to 10
It converges, to 3
It diverges: an infinite tail has no sum
It converges, to 7

why.correct: For $n \ge 100$, the tail's partial sums are $S_n - 7$, which approach $10 - 7 = 3$. Removing or adding finitely many terms never changes whether a series converges.
options: The first 99 terms add to 7; without them the sum is $10 - 7$.
Right: dropping finitely many terms keeps convergence and changes the sum by what was dropped.
The tail of a convergent series converges: its partial sums are $S_n - 7$.
7 is the sum of the dropped terms, not of the tail.
